Split on them as a player and a GM.

They tend to add to the flavor of a character and give the GM another plot hook, avenging a fallen AC/F or saving a diseased one. In combat, however, they seem to either be forgotten about or are used as a crutch.

If you go to a world where wizards are common there should be some understanding that killing the wizards pet lizard will severely hurt the wizard. As a player I try to kill enemy AC/Fs as a means of instantly weakening or getting the aggro of the NPC. If I do it as a GM the player tends to flip their shit, which is great because they are embracing their character. Still, it does suck to perma-fuck a person's character.

There seems to be four ways of thinking about it.

  1. Leave AC/F out of combat. They are purely a story driven element.
  2. They are fair targets. For those with the ability to cast spells through AC/F this is a trade off.
  3. Most players want a hybrid of the two options. The ability to act as a scout and cast spells via a beast, yet unable to sustain damage. This option is horse-shit.
  4. The AC/F is only in danger when being used. If the player forgets to bring their familiar into the encounter then it stays out. If they bring it into the encounter it stays in. This is my favorite option but it can be tedious in practice, players retroactively trying to bring their leopard into the caverns or up a wizard's tower.

Robert Jordan did a great job of balancing this with the wolves in TWoT (option 4). One of the main characters had a special connection with wolves. The wolves generally only advanced the plot. When they were used for in encounters they suffered casualties.
